evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: The proposal has already been successfully implemented in PyPy (Thanks @cfbolz  ). The target version is Python 3.14.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote:
Hi everyone ,

We are very exited to share with you PEP 768, which proposes adding a safe external debugger interface to CPython. We think this is a really exciting development that would allow debuggers and profilers to safely attach to running Python processes without stopping or restarting them.

evidence.author: CF Bolz-Tereick
evidence.quote: As can probably be seen by the fact that I’ve implemented this in PyPy already, I’m a strong +1 on this. I have wanted such a feature in PyPy since a long time, but never found a way to implement it that I was happy with, until @pablogsal described this idea to me a few weeks ago.

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: There’s some effort going towards making PyInterpreterState and PyThreadState structures lighter[1], so I feel like adding an unconditional 4KB to every instance might be a bit much. Any reason we can’t just make this a pointer (and perhaps allocate a static scratch buffer in PyRuntime)?

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: I’d also appreciate conditional compilation option to exclude the functionality entirely from a build (one of our $work requirements for production is to disable all debug interfaces)

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: We want to allow the user to select what Python thread executes what code, so technically the debugger may need to orchestrate different threads executing different code and for that we need 1 scratch buffer per thread.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: Makes sense. In any case note that there is not a lot of extra security to be gain here because if you can write to the process memory you already lost. We can look into that for sure. Maybe even a runtime option would also be useful.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: Yeah this is an excellent point. I will actually think I want to include it in the PEP

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: Hence the global scratch space that can be written to and then used as the pointer. But we would only have one 4KB space per process, rather than 4KB per thread.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: If you want, we can have an API (+ env var + whatever) that marks the memory as not writable so writing to it even if you have write permission will fail. That would need the application itself to call mprotect to remove the protections so you cannot do it from the outside.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: I penally would prefer to still allow one scratch pad per thread because I think the cost makes sense (and we can make it much smaller than 4k if we need) and also makes attaching easier because it needs less pointers to follow but if we think that is too costly I am happy with the scratchpad in PyRuntime instead.
Hence the global scratch space that can be written to and then used as the pointer. But we would only have one 4KB space per process, rather than 4KB per thread.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: If the debugger wants to attach without races, it should first send SIGSTOP to the process or use ptrace directly (as normal debuggers do), which requires similar permissions as process_vm_readv and friends.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: Oh, then this is a very interesting point because we could allow an even better way to attach to the process then without the need to send SIGSTOP to the process. We will investigate this idea in case we can leverage it.

evidence.author: Matt Wozniski
evidence.quote: I don’t see how. We can see if the lock is held from out of process, but we can’t lock it ourselves, as far as I can see. Without the ability to do an atomic compare-and-swap or something, there’s a TOCTOU issue there that I don’t see any way around: we check if it’s locked, we see that it isn’t, and we go to lock it ourselves, but whoopsie, someone else beat us to it and locked it from a different thread of execution and now both the debugger and a thread in the application think they own the lock.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: The gist is that that approach is fundamentally unsafe and can crash the process. The reason is that you cannot just inject code at arbitrary points of execution because the process can be in an inconsistent state.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: I am happy to mention it for sure but note that the approach is fundamentally different. Indeed the strategy that pyrasite uses has the same problems as the other tools mentioned in the PEP and those problems are covered as well in the text.

evidence.author: CF Bolz-Tereick
evidence.quote: I’d pick one of the names already being used, so perhaps debugger_script or debugger_pending_call would make sense.
it should definitely raise an audit event before executing any arbitrary code

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: I’d pick one of the names already being used, so perhaps debugger_script or debugger_pending_call would make sense.

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: The key thing this interface exposes is allowing an attacker to hide very easily. Assuming they have found a way to execute some amount of code on your system, unrelated to this interface[1], their goal is to persist by launching another process that won’t be detected by any defences.

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: Sure, you can say it won’t matter, but so will the next person, and the next after that. Eventually, it does matter.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: I am happy to add many ways to deactivate it in different times and in different ways including a compile time option, environment variables and more

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: Yes but also no: the code execution will be preceded by an audit interface. I could argue the other way: if an attacker manages to get code in this system then is the worse case for them because it will be super noisy as the audit system not only will show it but it can react to it stopping its execution.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: Not having this by default will greatly reduce the usefulness of most tools and will greatly hurt the development experience as things will not work by default.

evidence.author: Mark Shannon
evidence.quote: I think the PEP should address how we prevent: this PEP allowing attackers to avoid detection

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: The proposal includes a 4k buffer. All the talk about mprotect was just part of a specific idea that started as part of the discussion but is not part of the main proposal.

evidence.author: Mark Shannon
evidence.quote: I think a per-thread buffer would be better. Avoiding races on a global buffer will be tricky.
Avoiding races on a global buffer will be tricky.

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: More importantly, you can’t deterministically break into/connect to threads anyway, so calling into them one by one is essentially the same anyway.

evidence.author: Steve Dower
evidence.quote: Not from the point of view of a native debugger, which is what you are if you’re using these buffers. You have complete freedom to freeze and resume each thread.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: We have added a section explaining the deactivation mechanism based on a compile-time flag, a runtime environment variable and a -X option.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: We have added explicit mentions to the feature being gated via the interpreter’s audit API.

evidence.author: Pablo Galindo Salgado
evidence.quote: We have switched back to write a file to be executed in the buffer instead of the code itself. We have made this decision to address the in-process security scenarios, ensuring that an attacker with arbitrary memory write capabilities cannot escalate to arbitrary code execution.
